outline.chapter_title: 1. The Dispute, the Parties, and the Procedural Posture
outline.description: This chapter introduces the financed-insurance arrangement that gave rise to the case, the plaintiffs’ theory that GoAuto’s cancellations were ineffective, and the path from state-court class-action filing to Fifth Circuit review of summary judgment. It frames why the case turns on the mechanics of cancellation under Louisiana premium-finance law rather than on broader insurance bad-faith principles.
subtopics: The parties: former insureds Williams and Wright, accident plaintiff Jenkins, GoAuto, and premium-finance company APAC
How the premium-finance agreements worked: APAC paid the full premium and insureds repaid in installments
The power-of-attorney clause authorizing APAC to cancel policies upon default
The cancellations triggered by nonpayment
The lawsuit’s claims: ineffective cancellation, misrepresentation, and breach of good faith and fair dealing
Removal to federal court and the narrowing of the dispute to statutory compliance
The cross-motions for summary judgment and the district court’s ruling for GoAuto
The issues preserved on appeal: delivery of notice, GoAuto’s receipt of cancellation requests, and denial of plaintiffs’ partial summary judgment motion

outline.chapter_title: 2. Louisiana’s Statutory Scheme for Cancelling Financed Insurance Policies
outline.description: This chapter explains the specific Louisiana statute governing cancellation when a premium-finance company acts under a power of attorney. It focuses on the statutory text the Fifth Circuit parsed and the Louisiana cases emphasizing strict compliance, showing why small procedural details mattered so much in this appeal.
subtopics: La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a): what the premium-finance company must send to the insurer
The required certified statements: valid power of attorney, uncured default, prior notice to the insured, and notice to interested third parties
La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i): insurer action '[u]pon receipt' of the notice and statement
Why Louisiana courts demand strict adherence to statutory cancellation procedures
The consequences of noncompliance: defective process makes cancellation ineffective
The policies behind strict compliance identified in Louisiana cases: fixing the exact time of cancellation and preserving a minimum cure period
The interpretive challenge in this case: how strict compliance interacts with statutory silence on signatures and modern electronic processing

outline.chapter_title: 3. GoAuto and APAC’s Cancellation Procedure and the Core Compliance Questions
outline.description: This chapter reconstructs the operational steps used by APAC and GoAuto and identifies the two central legal questions the court had to answer: whether APAC’s unsigned electronic certification was sufficient, and whether GoAuto had legally 'received' the cancellation request before the automatic cancellation occurred.
subtopics: APAC’s ten-day notice to insureds after missed payment
Automatic e-mail transmission to GoAuto after the cure period expires
The contents of APAC’s cancellation request and certification language
GoAuto’s automated cancellation through its computer system upon receipt of the electronic request
The later ministerial step: an APAC employee affixes a signature stamp to printed documents
The pre-2017 and post-2017 paper-handling practices and shared filing/storage arrangements
Plaintiffs’ first theory: 'certifying' requires a signature before cancellation
Plaintiffs’ second theory: GoAuto did not actually 'receive' the request before cancellation
Why these factual details mattered to statutory validity and thus to all remaining claims

outline.chapter_title: 4. The Fifth Circuit’s Statutory Interpretation and Application
outline.description: This chapter tracks the court’s reasoning from statutory text to holding. It explains why the court rejected a signature requirement, accepted electronic receipt through GoAuto’s computer systems, and declined to expand strict-compliance doctrine beyond what the Louisiana statute expressly requires.
subtopics: The court’s starting point: the statute does not expressly require a signature
How the court interpreted 'certifying' as not necessarily requiring identification or signature by a specific employee
Treatment of Louisiana precedent: Delatte, Eaglin, Britten, and the limited guidance from KMJ Services, Hodges, Lewis, and Benitez
The court’s reading of Benitez: lack of signature was discussed as one flaw among several, not as an independent categorical defect
The principle that 'strict adherence' does not authorize courts to add procedural requirements absent from the statute
Interpretation of 'receipt' in § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i) using ordinary legal definitions from Black’s Law Dictionary
The role of automation: GoAuto’s web service as a means of taking possession, delivery, or custody of the request
Why electronic receipt by the insurer’s computer system satisfied the statute before cancellation
The court’s refusal to rely on the district court’s alternative 'private carrier' theory
The ultimate conclusion that GoAuto’s procedures complied with Louisiana law

outline.chapter_title: 5. Certification to the Louisiana Supreme Court, Disposition, and Case Significance
outline.description: This chapter explains the Fifth Circuit’s refusal to certify the statutory questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court, the resulting affirmance of summary judgment, and the practical significance of the opinion for financed-policy cancellations and electronically administered insurance practices.
subtopics: Plaintiffs’ request for certification and their argument about statewide importance
The Fifth Circuit’s general reluctance to certify absent a compelling reason
Why the mere absence of a Louisiana Supreme Court definition did not justify certification
How the court’s statutory-compliance holding resolved the appeal and supported denial of plaintiffs’ motion for partial summary judgment
The final disposition: affirmance of dismissal with prejudice of all claims against GoAuto
The case’s practical lesson about electronic communications and automated insurer systems under older statutory language
Its doctrinal significance: strict compliance remains mandatory, but courts will not invent extra statutory requirements
Implications for future litigants challenging financed-policy cancellations under Louisiana law
